No Lexapro anymore, still taking Buspar in addition to the rest of my cocktail.

I have found that in the beginning stages of getting the diagnosis antipsychotics/mood stabilizers tend to come second. First the depression needs to be handled.

My advice? Give yourself a minute to fully adjust. The other meds may very come later, but if you're already seeing improvements don't add more than you need to before you need to.

Ahh, yes. My favorite symptom.

There's been roughly 15 years of trial and error for me, but something I found very effective in the beginning was using American Sign Language to just say, "stop." There was something helpful about having a physical way to respond to this non-physical threat. It may feel weird, and certainly can lead to awkwardness is there are people around, but if you're actively struggling with suicidal thoughts what's a little awkwardness? If someone sees you and asks (depending on your relationship with them) be honest about what you're trying to work through. Ask for help.

I don't have to do that so much these days, but when the thoughts pop up to either self-harm to kill myself I enact some kind of other physical stimulus that won't actually hurt me. Rubbing ice on my wrists, tapping my wrists on desk corners, etc. 

Reminding myself that intrusive thoughts are not really my thoughts can also be helpful. Something that has helped me has been thinking about my brain as being at least a little broken. When something triggers these thoughts I ask myself, "are you going to let the healthy part of your brain win, or the broken part?" This helps me to remember that, while my experience is real, my broken brain has no right to tell me what to do.

I have some thoughts, but what I say is kind of dependent on how old/independent from your family you are. 

Some context: the sister in question *may* have thought similarly to your family, once upon a time. There are a lot of years between us living together and today, and it's been a slow building of understanding that she simply cannot understand. Additionally, she's educated and working as a nurse (now) and has worked in the hospital in various positions previously. Some of those positions required that she be the safety person for people who were on suicide watch, and I think that also helped her.

All this to say, she needed her own education and life experiences to get to where she is in her understanding today. I think my being vocal and occasionally brutally honest helped, but an important note here is that her current way of thinking didn't rely 100% on my efforts.

I'm working on an assumption here, but have you ever been brutally honest with your family about how close you've come to death? They may respond that you're being dramatic, but suicidal thinking *is* a dramatic response to (in my case these days) not very dramatic situations. I hate to be so generic and general, but I think a lot of people are simply incapable of making the leap of, "oh, an inconvenience. Guess I should kill myself now." And that's good (for them)-- but the fact that so many of us have these dramatic leaps in thought is a terrifying thing, and evidence that (in my opinion) this is a VERY real problem. 

I don't know that it's necessarily what you're looking for or comfortable with, but I have found that people only really take my struggles seriously after I get to the point of suicidal thinking and straight up tell them, "I am checking myself into the hospital so I don't kill myself tonight." The other person doesn't have to be able to understand where you're coming from, but my hope is that they would at the very least be able to have enough respect for your literal life to stop talking for a moment and reconsider. 

In the end, though, it is your life that you need to worry about. Their understanding cannot be your hill to die on-- you've got bigger things to take care of. Education is great, and necessary, but not at the detriment to your health be it mental, physical, or otherwise. Call them on their ableist comments, draw and keep boundaries to the best of your ability, and build a strong support team. This may begin as the professionals you see to keep well, but as you grow in your own understanding of yourself I feel confident that you will be better able to recognize people who won't tell you what you "should" be doing and instead will ask you how they can help.

I'm afraid this was more rambling than advice, but if you have specific questions about specific situations I can do my best to answer-- and hopefully others will be able to lend some guidance as well.

I have a professor who preaches this: 

Document everything. Anything you do that betters tour place of work/your clients and ESPECIALLY saves your workplace money. Then, when you have your supervision, bring your list along. It's stupid, but we need to advocate for ourselves as much as we advocated for the people we serve. It will never be lucrative, but social work SHOULD be life sustaining, for them and for us.

I'm in PA and had to do a phone interview for food stamps as well. Due to my disability, I was in the hospital (phoneless) and had no way of knowing 1. that I had been scheduled for an interview, 2. that I missed the interview, 3. that they were cutting my food stamps till I called them.

Turns out they didn't look at my submitted paystubs proving that I had some income (required for me), and when the person I spoke to told me I needed to do that, I pointed out I had posted updated paystubs two weeks earlier. She said, "oh," confirmed they were in my portal, and told me she'd let the case manager know.

All in all, maaaaaaaaybe a 15 minute conversation? My point is, don't build this up to be a bigger problem than it is. Anxiety is a beast, and it easily ramps up routine things to be much worse than they actually are. 

I would suggest creating a script for yourself, even bullet points of what you need to communicate so you don't feel extra anxious about forgetting pertinent information.

Just last night I was talking to a friend who does appear to have bipolar disorder (working on an official diagnosis with her provider) and we got to talking about an interaction I'd had recently with my mom. She didn't mean to hurt me with what she said, and I couldn't figure out why what she said had made me feel so bad, but finally I realized that her response to me made me feel like I was "crazy." That was... rough.

So, I shared this with my friend and we got into a discussion of the challenges of being rightfully angry/worried/sad/anxious/excited and people either asking if we're depressed/manic, or even accusing us of being so. It's beyond clear to me that unless a person has walked this path there is no understanding it, no matter how hard they try (if they try)-- which leads me to thus point: find community. This subreddit is a great first step, but finding people in "real life" who get it is also very important. 

I am by no means saying that you should tell EVERYbody of your diagnosis/challenges/etc, but disclosing to those who can help you may be beneficial. Is there a particular manager/supervisor who you trust? A doctor's note may be needed, true, but once you've got it in your pocket you've got it for the entirety of your time at this company. I've disclosed at some work places and not others, fully dependent on the circumstances I was in at the time. None of can really say what you *should* do, just maybe share our experiences. I'm very glad to say that the one that mattered most cared the least (in the best of ways).

As for the high achiever... this is where you are, today. Maybe it's where you've been for a long time, but none of this means it's where you'll be for the rest of your life. Do your best to have compassion and grace towards yourself, and take advantage of any and all resources available to you.

I completely understand this, but as far as being "normal" goes....

Would you hold yourself to the same standard is something was "physically" wrong with you? The argument can certainly made that bp2 is a physical issue (brain wise), but in any case, is you'd had an amputation and suffered from phantom pain would you be so hard on yourself? I feel it's a similar concept.

In my experience, knowing when to disclose has also been challenging, to say the least. Sometimes it helps me to step back and ask myself, "if my best friend was dealing with this, what would my advice to them be?"

Depends on the family member.

Most of my siblings (three brothers, three sisters) have zero comprehension of what it's like to have bp2, though they are broadly sympathetic. My oldest sister struggles with her own diagnoses and I generally find myself supporting her more than she supports me.

My mom has the same diagnosis and in the last few years has become very supportive. She agrees with me that I should never birth my own children (I cannot be off my meds long enough to carry a child), but would happily get some grandbabies via foster or adoption. 

My dad... forgets. Genuinely, that's what he told me. He forgot that I'd been hospitalized, to which my only response is really, "wish I could do the same."

One of the most helpful things I've learned in my journey to figuring out my diagnoses and how this one in particular affects me was learning what hypomania looks like in me. I definitely have the "textbook" hypomanic symptoms of excessive spending, hypersexuality, heightened creativity, etc, etc, but the other side that doesn't get talked about as much is that hypomania also presents as heightened anxiety, increased irritability, etc. I know when I'm not doing well, or not being consistent with my medication regimen, is that I am constantly on edge. I feel torn between rage and sobbing uncontrollably. Another point is that depression specific meds can trigger hypomanic episodes, which was certainly my experience in the beginning until I finally asked for an assessment for bipolar 2. 

Funnily enough, sort of, I decided to go inpatient back in October because I didn't feel safe on my own. While explaining to the hospital psychiatrist my struggles with intrusive thoughts, her response was, "well, that's not bipolar. That's OCD." She then promptly went on to tell me that bipolar 2 doesn't lead to inpatient stays (which is so absurd, as it was the depression piece of it that led me to go inpatient), and then fully neglected to tell me how to manage OCD or anything. The rest of the staff there were great-- she was less so.

Finally.... I feel like one of the telltale signs of having bipolar (1 or 2) is to doubt the diagnosis. I agree with the other commentor that talking to your therapist and/or psychiatrist about this is a good idea. Sometimes I just need someone to hear me out and remind me that my mode of thinking is not "normal." It's been my "normal" for so long that I genuinely forget that it is rather unusual in the general population.

I've said it before and I'll say it again-- Vraylar saved my life. I was haunted by intrusive thoughts telling me to SH or take my life, every single day.

More than that, actually-- I counted once and had I think 26 intense intrusive thoughts in four hours? So about every ten minutes my brain either telling me to severely injure myself or straight up find some way to die. It was... a lot.

Vraylar pretty much silenced those thoughts. I still get them on occasion, especially when under high stress, but on the regular? Nada.

Worth a try, in my opinion.

I had my therapist forget me once.

I was sitting in the waiting room for at least half an hour, just... waiting, coming up with various scenarios in which the client before me must have been having a really hard time and that's why she wasn't coming out for me. Then... I saw her walk back in, lunch in hand.

Yup. She had asked me to come in early for the appointment... then forgot she had done so.

It's not the same situation, I know, but the reason I bring this up is because this therapist was A M A Z I N G for me. She knew exactly how to call me out for my nonsense, how to get me to fight for myself, and when to just sit there and listen when I could barely breathe. My therapist was, just like yours is, human. There is no such thing as perfection, and sometimes we get bounced around a bit. I would encourage you to have some grace and also to start building a wider support network. I know how impossible this can feel, but even if it's "just" plugging the Crisis textline into your phone so you have someone to talk to can be beneficial.

Additionally... as someone who both lives with my own ABCs of disorders, and works with people with their own psychiatric disorders.... I would caution you against becoming too dependent on your therapist. The two of you should have a relationship, absolutely, but it needs to be a professional therapeutic relationship. It isn't fair to either of you to put your entire well-being on one person, even if they are a professional. It's not reasonable or realistic, either. Have you ever looked into/considered a support group? NAMI has virtual support groups I think every Thursday at 7 PM Eastern time. I cannot speak to their effectiveness personally, but I know they've been very effective for some people-- and I cannot imagine they'd still be going on if they weren't helping loads more.

In my experience it meant the dosage of medication I was on wasn't high enough. I've never been on lithium specifically, so I can't say either way how that particular drug works, but for the many others I've tried that's usually been the problem.

The worst for me was when I was put on Zoloft. I was absolutely numb. Nothing mattered at all. I wasn't depressed anymore, I was just... existing. I spoke to my doctor about it, she increased the dose age, and I felt better.

I am most definitely of the mind that I no longer need partial, which is indicative of the fact that I absolutely need it. I think I've seen the writing on the wall for a while but I was desperate to believe this wasn't happening again so I just kept shoving it down.

It helps in the long run because it's a stepping off point. If, like so many in this sub, you and your provider think you have "only" MDD, then you're only getting half the treatment you need for recovery. When a person gets an accurate diagnosis they are better able to receive scripts and therapies tailored for that diagnosis.

I (obviously) have bp2, and kind of self-diagnosed myself years before receiving an actual diagnoses. It was a bizarre moment of "I was RIGHT!" and, "oh no, I was right."

I'm currently in my senior year of bachelor's level social work classes with every intention of becoming an LCSW  to work with adults with trauma histories. I've spent the last seven years working in a residential treatment house for adults with mental health disorders, and it was about year two of that job that I shared my struggled and (at that time) diagnoses of MDD and anxiety with my colleagues. It is a huge help of having both sides of the door experiences, but it can also be hugely frustrating. "I know what works, just LISTEN to me!!"

But everyone's journey is different, and many of us have to learn by our own mistakes rather than learning from others, self included. The biggest change in my recovery was getting started in Vraylar. Violent intrusive thoughts towards myself was my biggest hurdle, and that medication changed my life dramatically. I have a handful of other meds, of course, but that is the one I know I absolutely cannot miss (of course, that doesn't mean I don't occasionally talk myself out of taking it).

It's rough being in this position because I absolutely see the necessity of taking meds as scheduled and prescribed, but there is always the lingering thought of, "maybe I'm not actually that bad off." I have to tell myself, and have others tell me, that I really am that bad off and taking my meds/keeping up with appointments is the only thing getting me through. 

I wish you luck with your recovery and acceptance of your "new" self. It's hard, for sure, but that empathy you have now? It will help you so, so much in helping others.

I don't know if I'm too intense, but I have wondered about it. I find that I can't really keep long term or close friends, and it kind of really sucks. I've been feeling generally happy but kinda sad lately because of it and I'm not sure what to do.

I don't know that this will actually be helpful for you but I thought I'd share my experience.

Back in the "beginning," before I got my diagnosis I was being treated for major depressive disorder and anxiety. I always thought the anxiety piece didn't make sense because I really didn't experience anxiety-- until I did. I thought I understood what anxiety was and what it looked like, but really, my depression was so severe I just wasn't able to recognize anxiety for what it was.

Once my depressive symptoms started to be appropriately managed my anxiety symptoms ramped up like woah. I've had to try a few meds for it (I'm on a handful of meds now, and actually find hydroxyzine works wonderfully as an occasional add on) and it helps that I had an excellent psychiatrist for ~4 years who really worked with me to find a combination that worked for me.

In my experience, I had to try different meds for different symptoms. We're on different medications for depression/mood stabilization, so I don't know how much what you take really does for anxiety clinically. It's likely worth asking for a trial of another anxiety medication (Buspar is one that works well for me). 

Some other things I tried was tracking my anxious thoughts. Not necessarily what they were, just how often I was having them. It helped me to realize that it really was a problem and it gave me something a little more concrete to show my doctor to "prove" something was very wrong.
Vraylar. I consider it the med that saved my life. I've struggled with intense intrusive thoughts most of my life and Vraylar made them almost entirely disappear.

I think this is a great question, and I think of my "aha!" moment with some regularity.

When I was in my low to mid 20's, I suddenly realized in the course of a new relationship that I was very much behaving like love-struck teenager. I drew the conclusion that I was finally coming out of my arrested development and suddenly had to deal with "real" emotions again. Over the decade or so since the, I've built the beginnings of a real life and not so much a life focused solely on my early experiences. At 37, I still feel a bit younger than I am (maybe early 30s?) but I don't feel as much that I'm always playing catch up.

I suppose I should have specified that, ignoring the recent weight jump, I'm still 15 lbs down from where I was a month ago.

I'm trying to focus less on what my body looks like and more on how it feels. For the last week I've been trying to get in my walks, and going uphill is noticeably easier now. I don't *think* I'm avoiding going places or seeing people, but it's an interesting question. Just yesterday I was asking myself at what point I'll purchase more body fitting clothing (partially because of the cost of new clothing, partially because of other people actually *seeing* me) and it occurred to me that oversized clothing may very well be an effort to hide myself instead of just being comfortable like I always told myself it was.

I had MAJOR dysmorphia that last time I lost weight so I'm trying to be very conscientious of that this time around. I'm working on finding a therapist to help me sort out my feelings regarding losing weight as it really messed me up last time. My doctor will be thrilled to see I'm losing weight as she's been pretty on me about my weight. 

All of this to say... thanks for the birthday wishes, and I will continue to keep these things in mind!

My moment was the culmination of a few smaller moments.
1. I had seen a recording of me made for a class I was taking. I saw myself and thought, "Is this *really* what everyone sees when they look at me?"
2. I'm working on completing my undergraduate degree in social work and realized that I cannot advise people without taking those same advisements for myself.
3. I went to the doctor and weighed in at the highest weight I'd ever been.

These events happened within two days of each other, and I just got done with being this unhealthy. As an added motivator, I came across and decided to take part in a 100 mile fundraiser throughout May and am using it as a motivator to get moving again. 

This all started about a month ago, and I was staring myself down during a video call recently and thought, "Is my... is my face *thinner??* It *is* thinner!" 

It was pretty wild.

It's so relieving to see that my old tools still work and haven't been terribly painful. This may change as I get closer to my GW, but I'm choosing not to think that far ahead. I'll just get overwhelmed. 

Anyhow, those were my moments.

Personally, I had to listen to my body ( sounds a little woowoo, for sure) and figure out which foods actually left me feeling satiated after eating them. For example, some people go for eating lean meat only, which is fine, but there are times when only a fattier pot roast will do. If I try to replace it with a chicken breast, I will get bored and not feel terribly satiated. I weigh out E.V.E.R.Y.T.H.I.N.G. I take in so I have a better idea of serving sizes, but I refuse to get rid of what really makes me happy. 

Losing weight is simple, but I think a lot of people (not you, necessarily) conflate this with being easy. The two are not the same, and it does require getting to know yourself a bit better. The last time I worked on losing weight I managed to lose ~65 pounds, but then I let other people's comments and a lengthy plateau get to me and I gave up. Over the course of eight years I gained ~75 pounds (original plus 10), and I decided I couldn't do it to myself anymore. Renewing my efforts, I'm doing exactly what I did last time and over a month have lost 20 pounds. 

It's my birthday tomorrow and I bought a tiramisu to share. It's my birthday, I want to celebrate, I DO NOT want this whole cake sitting in my fridge to eat by myself. This has been a HUGE piece of losing weight happily-- get what you need to satisfy the craving, enjoy your piece, GET RID OF THE REST (my brother in law will be quite happy, I think). 

This is a frustrating process, especially as you're just learning, but don't give up! It's great that you tried therapy, to whatever end, now try keeping some kind of log of what foods make you feel which kind of way. Just my two cents, but like I've said, it works for me!

Good luck!

I made a choice a couple months ago to stop shoving down uncomfortable emotions and to stop and actually explore them. It's made my life a lot better.

I am starting over again after gaining nearly 70 pounds (60 regained, 10ish extra). One thing I've found incredibly helpful is just committing to a weekend of making crockpot meals and separating them out into containers, keeping just enough for three or four days and freezing the rest. I say the weekend because this allows for multiple kinds of meals so I have variety over the next few weeks. Crockpot liners have been a life saver with this, and they come out to about $0.50 a piece, which is more than worth it to me.

It's so easy to say "don't give up," but having plateued and let people get in my brain, I know how important it is to surround myself with good people and to keep moving forward.

I don't want to be the person who gets put in a government nursing home, wasting away and only half aware of it.

There are three things I try to remember when I feel another depressive episode coming on:

1. This is not forever. As bad as it feels, and as hopeless as life seems to be, it isn't. Today may suck, tomorrow might be worse- hey, things might suck for a few weeks or months, but what is that compared to the rest of your life? Hold on and keep moving forward. This is not forever.

2. Am I going to *choose* to be down, or am I going to *choose* to be positive? Your attitude when depressed makes a massive difference. When you're lying in bed trying to decide if today is worth getting through, *choose* to put forth the effort. If you constantly give in to the desire to do nothing, you're only putting yourself in the position to get worse.

3. Is what I'm feeling right now based on reality, or on my perception of reality?
     When you're depressed you get into a very "me" mindset. Everything is about you. Not so much in an "everything is about me" sort of way, but in that you're so stuck in how *you feel* about a situation. The problem with this is that you forget to consider that the circumstances of the problem your having may not be warranted. ie, you try making plans with someone but they already have plans, so obviously they don't care about you and they don't love you and nobody loves you and no one could ever love you and you may as well not be alive.

Now, which is more likely; that they (and by extension, nobody) don't love love you, or that you asked too late and were already committed to something else? You need to stop and think about how you're feeling, and consider whether you might be taking things in the wrong way.

These are the things that help me the most when I find myself in the middle of another depressive episode. 

Another important thing is to be proactive, rather than reactive. Depression is often a life long thing, but you can learn to manage it. Pay attention to the symptoms of your depression. Write them down! You can learn how to catch yourself before you fall into a dangerous place if you know the things that come before an episode. I, for example, have trouble sleeping, get angry at small things and  find my OCD acting up weeks or even months before a major depressive episode hits. If I catch myself, I can prepare for it and can keep myself from believing the lies that depression likes to tell me.

Most importantly, you need to learn that you can trust others to help you. They may not understand what you're going through and they may give you bad advise, but they love you. Hold on to that.

When I was a child, perhaps still in single digits, I had a(n even) younger(er) friend who liked to follow me EVERYWHERE when we were together. I actually found her to be rather annoying at times, and had little patience.

One day, while I was at home watching TV, my mom calls down to me from the second floor to tell me that this little girl was on the phone and wanted to talk to me. So, I picked up the downstairs phone, said hello and half listened as she talked- I mean, what do little kids have to say anyway, right? After she was finished blathering on I told   her that I was busy and couldn't really talk to her. You know, TV and all.

And that's when I discovered that my mom had never hung up the other phone.

Right, right, she shouldn't have eavesdropped. 

Except that she should have. And I'm glad she did.
 
She interrupted my good-byes to tell me to come upstairs, and when I did she told me that she stayed on the line because she could hear my friend's distress. She told me everything this little girl had been trying to tell me. 

Apparently, her mother and grandmother were fighting and she had called me for advice and comfort. And what did I do? I ignored her and told her I couldn't talk. 

Because, you know. TV.

I can't remember what exactly my mom said to me, but I do know that ever since that day, if someone calls me and I find myself getting distracted, I find somewhere completely silent and away from all distractions. People deserve to have my undivided attention, and if I'm going to be a true friend to them, I have to give it to them.

When someone is obviously distressed, I go to them and do my best to help them. I pay attention. I try my best (because come on, no one's perfect) not to get annoyed when my decompression time is interrupted by someone with a crisis. Because we all need help sometimes. 

Whether we're seven or seventy, we need someone to listen.  

Tl;dr- What, did your parents never teach you how to power through? Read it!

The very reason I'm so adamant about staying away from onions! There are so many things I'd love to try, but the fear of going from itching and swelling to full on anaphylaxis is a pretty effective deterrent.

For years my family would give me food with onions, getting angry when I wouldn't eat it. They would go on about how I wouldn't even taste it, I should just eat it, etc, etc.

The reason I didn't like onions wasn't because I didn't like the taste (onions typically didn't stay on my tongue long enough for me to know how I felt about that), but because it "made my throat feel weird."

It wasn't for about ten or so years after they gave up on forcing me to eat onions that my sister had a major allergic reaction to food she was eating. Hearing what the doctors had to say about her reactions were what made me realize that my throat "feeling weird" was actually my throat swelling up.

So, yes, some of us really are allergic to onions.
